items.title: Identifying a Possible Second Equation in a System With No Solutions

key_prerequisites.name: Systems of Equations With No Solutions and Infinitely Many Solutions

sections.normalized_html:
One of the two equations in a linear system is [MATH: -8x - 4y = 12.] The system has no solution. Which of the following could be the other equation in the system?

  1. [MATH: 2x + y = 5]

  2. [MATH: 8x + 4y = -12]

  3. [MATH: -2x + y = 7]

  4. [MATH: x - 2y = 1]
sections.readable_text:
One of the two equations in a linear system is [MATH: -8x - 4y = 12.] The system has no solution. Which of the following could be the other equation in the system?

1. [MATH: 2x + y = 5]
2. [MATH: 8x + 4y = -12]
3. [MATH: -2x + y = 7]
4. [MATH: x - 2y = 1]

sections.normalized_html:
A system of linear equations has no solution if the equations represent parallel lines that never intersect. This occurs when both equations have the same slope but different [MATH: y]-intercepts.

Let’s start by rewriting the given equation in slope-intercept form, [MATH: y = mx + b{:}] [MATH: − 8x − 4y|= 12; − 4y|= 8x + 12; y|= − 2x − 3]

So the given equation has slope [MATH: -2] and [MATH: y]-intercept [MATH: -3.]

Let's now look for a second equation among the choices that has the same slope but a different [MATH: y]-intercept. We consider the choices in turn.

  • Consider the equation [MATH: 8x + 4y = -12] and rewrite it in slope-intercept form: [MATH: y = -2x - 3] This equation has the same slope and the same [MATH: y]-intercept as the given equation. It is not valid.

  • Consider the equation [MATH: -2x + y = 7] and rewrite it in slope-intercept form: [MATH: y = 2x + 7] This equation has a different slope, [MATH: m = 2 \ne -2.] Therefore, it is not valid.

  • Consider the equation [MATH: x - 2y = 1] and rewrite it in slope-intercept form: [MATH: y = \dfrac{1}{2}x - \dfrac{1}{2}] This equation has a different slope, [MATH: m = \dfrac{1}{2} \ne -2.] Therefore, it is not valid.

  • Consider the equation [MATH: 2x + y = 5] and rewrite it in slope-intercept form: [MATH: y = -2x + 5.] This equation has the same slope, [MATH: m = -2,] and a different [MATH: y]-intercept, [MATH: b=5\neq - 3.] Therefore, it is valid.

Consequently, the second equation in the system could be [MATH: 2x + y = 5.]

Therefore, the correct answer is only I.

sections.normalized_html:
A system of linear equations has no solution if the equations represent parallel lines that never intersect. This occurs when both equations have the same slope but different [MATH: y]-intercepts.

Let’s analyze each system:

  • [MATH: {y = − 3; y = x − 3] The first equation is a horizontal line, so it has slope [MATH: 0;] the second has slope [MATH: 1.] The slopes are different, so the lines intersect at one point.

[MATH: \qquad] Thus, this system has one solution.

  • [MATH: {y = − 2x + 3; y = 2x − 5] The slopes are different ([MATH: -2] and [MATH: 2]), so the lines intersect at one point.

[MATH: \qquad] Thus, this system has one solution.

  • [MATH: {x = 6; y = − 1] This system contains a vertical line and a horizontal line. These lines intersect at exactly one point.

[MATH: \qquad] Thus, this system has one solution.

  • [MATH: {y = 5x + 9; y = 5x − 4] Both equations have slope [MATH: 5,] but different [MATH: y]-intercepts ([MATH: 9] and [MATH: -4]). These lines are parallel and distinct, so they never intersect.

[MATH: \qquad] Thus, this system has no solution.

Therefore, the correct answer is only II.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Item 2 — Example: Identifying a Possible Second Equation in a System With No Solutions

Example Prompt:
One of the two equations in a linear system is [MATH: -8x - 4y = 12.] The system has no solution. Which of the following could be the other equation in the system?

1. [MATH: 2x + y = 5]
2. [MATH: 8x + 4y = -12]
3. [MATH: -2x + y = 7]
4. [MATH: x - 2y = 1]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A system of linear equations has no solution if the equations represent parallel lines that never intersect. This occurs when both equations have the same slope but different [MATH: y]-intercepts.

Let’s start by rewriting the given equation in slope-intercept form, [MATH: y = mx + b{:}]
[MATH: − 8x − 4y|= 12; − 4y|= 8x + 12; y|= − 2x − 3]

So the given equation has slope [MATH: -2] and [MATH: y]-intercept [MATH: -3.]

Let's now look for a second equation among the choices that has the same slope but a different [MATH: y]-intercept. We consider the choices in turn.

- Consider the equation [MATH: 8x + 4y = -12] and rewrite it in slope-intercept form:
[MATH: y = -2x - 3]
This equation has the same slope and the same [MATH: y]-intercept as the given equation. It is not valid.
- Consider the equation [MATH: -2x + y = 7] and rewrite it in slope-intercept form:
[MATH: y = 2x + 7]
This equation has a different slope, [MATH: m = 2 \ne -2.] Therefore, it is not valid.
- Consider the equation [MATH: x - 2y = 1] and rewrite it in slope-intercept form:
[MATH: y = \dfrac{1}{2}x - \dfrac{1}{2}]
This equation has a different slope, [MATH: m = \dfrac{1}{2} \ne -2.] Therefore, it is not valid.
- Consider the equation [MATH: 2x + y = 5] and rewrite it in slope-intercept form:
[MATH: y = -2x + 5.]
This equation has the same slope, [MATH: m = -2,] and a different [MATH: y]-intercept, [MATH: b=5\neq - 3.] Therefore, it is valid.

Consequently, the second equation in the system could be
[MATH: 2x + y = 5.]

Therefore, the correct answer is only I.

Item 5 — Example: Identifying a System With No Solution

Which of the following systems of linear equations has no solution?

Explanation:
A system of linear equations has no solution if the equations represent parallel lines that never intersect. This occurs when both equations have the same slope but different [MATH: y]-intercepts.

Let’s analyze each system:

- [MATH: {y = − 3; y = x − 3]
The first equation is a horizontal line, so it has slope [MATH: 0;] the second has slope [MATH: 1.] The slopes are different, so the lines intersect at one point.

[MATH: \qquad] Thus, this system has one solution.

- [MATH: {y = − 2x + 3; y = 2x − 5]
The slopes are different ([MATH: -2] and [MATH: 2]), so the lines intersect at one point.

[MATH: \qquad] Thus, this system has one solution.

- [MATH: {x = 6; y = − 1]
This system contains a vertical line and a horizontal line. These lines intersect at exactly one point.

[MATH: \qquad] Thus, this system has one solution.

- [MATH: {y = 5x + 9; y = 5x − 4]
Both equations have slope [MATH: 5,] but different [MATH: y]-intercepts ([MATH: 9] and [MATH: -4]). These lines are parallel and distinct, so they never intersect.

[MATH: \qquad] Thus, this system has no solution.

Therefore, the correct answer is only II.
